Just for my own clarity. ...

Let's assume that there is a third party watching two separate civilizations. One located near the galaxy's edge and the other located much closer toward the center. From the perspective of this third party, both civilizations appear at the same moment.

Would it make sense to then say that the third party would watch the development & advancement of the inner civilization occuring at a faster rate than those within the outer civilization?
It would be the other way around. Gravity slows time, so the planet closer to the center would appear to be living in slow motion.

You might age half as fast relative to a distant observer, but you'd also function half as fast. The only advantage would be that you would get to see more of the future happening outside your local area. The actual amount of life would be the same for you, presuming the tidal effects of the gravity didn't shorten your life.

Now because of this, would it plausable to think that relative to the rest of the milky way, earth will be the fastest advancing civilization because we are essentially in fast motion in comparison to the rest of our galaxy on account of our location at the edge of the galaxy?

Alas, no. A civilization somehow finding itself on a planet near the center of the galaxy, orbiting a star that is itself orbiting the central black hole at a rapid rate, would experience greater time dilation due to the gravity well they are in. They would also need much higher levels of technology to escape such a gravity well. Both effects would set them back considerably as a space-faring race, so chances are that's not a good place to look for them. Time dilation means although you get to watch longer, the other side gets to act faster, but having your environment shredded by tidal forces constantly is a much bigger problem.

Also, we're not really going much faster -- or slower -- than the rest of the galaxy. The baffling flatness of galaxy rotation curves was one of the key clues that dark matter exists.

It is plausible but not necessarily correct to believe that other civilizations will more likely than not come from regions of the galactic disk similar to our own, because we have enough star formation and death to churn out the necessary elements, but not so much as to repeatedly sterilize the planetary systems that get created. This, however, is based on "life as we know it" and most reasonable extrapolations. I personally suspect there is life-as-we-don't-know-it (and may not even recognize as life unless it wants to announce itself) in conditions we could never have imagined to be hospitable to life, but it's really somewhat pointless to even speculate on what that might be, or where it may be found, unless you just want to write a good story.
